items.title: [pbs.org] Super El Niño nears December peak as extreme weather spreads
items.content_html: The exceptionally strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is intensifying weather risks across several regions, including heavy rain and flash floods in the U.S. Southwest. Scientists say the pattern adds moisture to the air and shifts winds, making downpours more likely, although it is not the sole cause of individual storms. The World Meteorological Organization expects the event to peak in December and persist into February 2027. The agency says it could rank among the strongest since at least 1950. Flooding has also been reported in Peru and Ecuador, while Indonesia and parts of Southeast Asia are unusually dry. In the Southwest, flooding prompted evacuations, and the San Juan River threatened Pagosa Springs, Colorado. Warmer oceans linked to human-caused climate change may amplify the event’s effects, but scientists caution that separating El Niño’s contribution from the long-term warming trend remains difficult. In September, sea-surface temperature in the Pacific’s Niño 3.4 reference region reached 29.70°C, while the global ocean average for that month, excluding polar waters, set a September record of 21.05°C. Forecasters expect the strongest effects to continue into 2027.

items.title: [taz.de] Sierra Club projects data centers could add 618 million tons of CO2
items.content_html: A Sierra Club analysis estimates that power generation for U.S. data centers planned between 2025 and 2030 could emit 618 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, nearly matching Germany’s reported annual emissions. Those added emissions could push U.S. power-sector emissions 42% above 2025 levels by 2030, erasing reductions made since 2011, according to the analysis. About 460 million metric tons of the projected annual emissions would come from gas generators built or contracted to serve data centers off the public grid, according to the analysis. The estimate covers proposed and pending projects. An energy-policy expert said the outcome is possible but not inevitable.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

items.title: [climatechangenews.com] COP17 urges subsidy cuts as nature finance gap persists before COP31
items.content_html: Governments at the U.N. biodiversity summit, COP17, agreed to accelerate efforts to cut subsidies that damage nature, including support for fossil fuels, but left unresolved how to fund conservation. Nearly 200 countries adopted the Yerevan Pathway in Armenia after the first review found the world off track on almost all biodiversity goals for 2030. The agreement calls for countries to revise their biodiversity plans to address gaps in marine, coastal and inland-water protection and accelerate efforts to reduce harmful incentives by at least $500 billion a year by 2030. Developed countries missed a commitment to provide at least $20 billion annually for nature by 2025, while environmental funding is projected to fall 27% over 2026-30, Carbon Brief reported. Organizers said governments, philanthropies and investors announced more than $1.8 billion in nature finance at the summit, compared with the framework’s goal of mobilizing $200 billion a year by 2030. Countries invited non-donor states to express interest in joining the donor list, but deferred a decision on the structure of a permanent post-2030 financing mechanism until COP18 in Quito in 2028. The U.N. climate conference COP31 begins in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 9.

items.title: [independent.co.uk] Oil majors report wartime profit surge as climate groups demand windfall taxes
items.content_html: Six major European oil companies earned a combined $89 billion in the first nine months of 2026, more than twice their earnings a year earlier. U.S. oil and gas companies made more than $130 billion from April through September, nearly three times their earnings in the same period last year. The companies benefited from higher oil prices and refining margins after the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran disrupted energy supplies and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Climate campaigners called for windfall taxes, arguing the revenue should cushion households against energy costs and extreme weather and support a shift to cleaner energy. The oil and gas industry opposes a European Union-wide levy, warning it could weaken investment and energy security. The EU is considering such a tax, while Portugal has already imposed a 33% levy on extraordinary 2026 profits. Companies have largely used windfalls to reduce debt and return money to shareholders rather than increase production spending.

items.title: [agrarzeitung.de] Drought, heat and winter damage cut 2026 farm output across regions
items.content_html:
🌾 🔭 ✏️

Weather extremes damaged crops and forage across Europe and South Asia in 2026, with drought and heat reducing yields and a cold winter with little snow harming Sweden’s autumn-sown grains. France’s sunflower harvest was estimated at 1.2 million tonnes, 14% below 2025, while Boerenbond estimated €260 million in losses for Flemish farmers and growers. In Baden-Württemberg, summer rainfall totaled 156 mm, about 45% below the 1961-1990 average; the state farmers’ association estimated forage losses at 30% to 40%, reaching 50% in the worst-hit locations. In Maharashtra’s Shevgaon area, drought has reduced fodder availability, while mechanized sugarcane harvesting removes a traditional source of green feed. Farmers say their livestock are producing less milk. Following late-September rain, Baden-Württemberg farmers are assessing whether grassland has recovered and whether reseeded areas will need further repair after winter.
